executive_summary: GBP/CHF closed at 1.09734 on 2 October 2026, so one pound buys 1.09734 francs and a rising pair means a stronger pound. It is up 0.47% over one month, 1.60% over three, 3.31% over six and 2.83% over twelve. That puts it at the 85th percentile of its 52-week closing range. On 1 October the pair printed its 52-week high of 1.11079, at the lower edge of a ten-touch resistance band, and then fell 142 pips to close at 1.09662. The pair is driven by carry. The policy differential is 375bp, Bank Rate at 3.75% against an SNB at 0.00%, and the executable futures roll is 441.4bp a year. Bank of America has argued that "no major G10 cross offers higher vol-adjusted carry", making GBP/CHF particularly attractive as currency-market volatility continues to decline through the summer. The two dossiers are both bearish against the dollar, sterling at −0.0583 and the franc at −0.3002, and on the cross those views net to a positive differential. The settled verdict is Tactical Bullish (score +0.2309, conviction 3) and Strategic Neutral (score +0.0398, conviction 2). Strategically, a carry gap that widens to 400bp is offset almost exactly by an 11.7 percentage-point current-account gap and a 93.8% versus 38.5% debt-to-GDP gap. On the chart, spot sits 63 pips below a slowly declining 200-week average at 1.10362, with the daily averages stacked bullishly underneath (50-day 1.0956, 100-day 1.08299, 200-day 1.07021). The main caveat is that the level map is less generous than the score. The tactical base case pays 77 pips against a 233-pip downside case, and the trade is positive in expectation only once roughly 37 pips of four-week roll is counted. Size it below what the conviction-3 headline suggests and treat 28 October as an event that moves both legs against the position at once.

market_context.valuation_assessment: No pair-level PPP series exists. The REER-relative proxy used in both dossiers puts sterling's BIS broad real effective rate at 112.33 against the franc's 99.87, both for August 2026. On that basis sterling is about 12.5% rich against the franc in relative real terms, and closing the gap entirely would imply roughly 0.9756 on the current spot. The proxy says something about structure, not timing. Sterling's real rate is the third richest of eleven and has barely moved over the year, while the franc's is 2.83% lower year on year. The current level therefore prices a richly valued deficit currency against a cheapening surplus one, and the 375bp carry is what compensates the holder. Valuation gives no tactical trigger. Strategically it caps the upside, because any rally driven by Bank of England hike repricing pushes an already rich real exchange rate higher. Spot sits at the 84th percentile of the 52-week intraday range (1.02857 to 1.11079) and the 85th of the closing range (1.03555 to 1.10859); the sterling dossier's 97th closing percentile at the 29 September close of 1.10319 is out of date after the 1 October reversal.

market_context.recent_regime: For six months GBP/CHF has been a carry grind: from 1.05648 on 6 April to a closing high of 1.10859 on 30 September. Two shocks interrupted it. On 19 August the pair fell 1.3% in a 157-pip session, and on 1 October it reversed 142 pips from the 1.11079 high. The one-day drops are steep and the recoveries are slow, which is the payoff shape of a carry trade. The story behind it is policy divergence. The SNB held at zero on 24 September while the MPC voted 6-3 to hold with three members wanting a hike, and Swiss September CPI on 1 October showed data in line with market expectations and nowhere close to pressuring the SNB to alter its accommodative monetary policy. Even so, the pair has not managed a sustained hold above its 200-week average, and the ten-touch band at 1.10955–1.11969 has now rejected it on first contact.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy carry is +375bp in sterling's favour: Bank Rate is 3.75% (as of 2026-09-28) and the SNB rate is 0.00% (as of 2026-09-29). The executable carry is wider. The store's CME calendar-spread cross gives a GBP/CHF roll of −441.4bp annualised, observed 2026-09-30 over 74.7 to 165.6 days. A negative roll means the forward curve discounts the pair, so a rolled long collects about 4.41% a year. The 66.4bp gap over the policy differential is cross-currency basis plus term effects, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve; it is not reported as a basis quote. Eurex lists GBP/CHF futures and the visible strip slopes steeply downward (Dec 2026 1.02377 against a March 2027 contract at 1.01292). Carry-to-vol: the first pass gives 0.75 on policy carry over the store's 4.969% three-month estimate, with an honest range of 0.64–0.75; on the executable roll it is 0.89. Against the payload's realised volatility the policy-carry ratio is 0.66 on the 20-day figure (5.65%) and 0.70 on the 60-day figure (5.38%), and on the roll 0.78 and 0.82. Whichever measure is used, this is the best risk-adjusted carry in the sterling complex. Carry is working on this pair and has worked for six months: the pair is up 3.31% on spot alone and roughly 5.5% including roll. The regime breaks on a volatility event, and when it does it hits the pair from both sides at once: the franc is the haven, and sterling has a dated fiscal binary.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +375bp in sterling's favour, Bank Rate at 3.75% against an SNB policy rate of 0.00%, and the gated payload confirms it as a policyDifferential of 3.75. That is the widest positive carry sterling earns against any G10 counterpart and the third widest the franc pays, behind only AUD at 460bp and NOK at 450bp. The executable number is wider still: the store's futures calendar-spread cross prices the GBP/CHF roll at -441.4bp annualised on 2026-09-30, so the forward curve discounts the pair by about 4.4% a year and a rolled long collects roughly that, some 66bp more than the policy differential, the residual being cross-currency basis and term effects that cannot be separated without an OIS curve and which are therefore not reported as a basis quote. The trajectory is widening on both legs. The MPC held 6-3 on 17 September with Greene, Mann and Pill voting for 4.00% and nobody voting to cut, and the market prices close to 80% for a 25bp rise on 5 November; the SNB held at zero for a fifth consecutive assessment on 24 September with a conditional inflation forecast of 0.7, 0.8 and 0.8 per cent for 2026 to 2028 constructed explicitly on an unchanged 0% rate. The transmission is simply that at 375bp this pair is a carry trade before it is anything else. The timing point that matters tactically is that neither leg has a scheduled decision inside a four-week window: the gated meeting file puts the BoE at 5 November, thirty-five days from the valuation date, and the SNB at 10 December, seventy days out. The differential can therefore only be repriced by data inside the window, not delivered, and the two front ends carry opposite repricing risks — the Swiss 2-year has added 19bp of hike pricing that the SNB's own published forecast says is unnecessary, while the UK front end is merely over-hawkish relative to a hike the Committee has already signalled.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential almost certainly widens rather than narrows, and this is the one factor on which the two dossiers agree without qualification: the sterling dossier names GBP/CHF explicitly as widening to +400bp on its base case, and the franc dossier has the SNB at zero through the horizon with core inflation at 0.40% and nominal wage growth at 0.40%. A Bank Rate of 4.00% delivered on 5 November, with a residual path toward 4.25% if services inflation holds near 3.4%, against an SNB whose three-year conditional forecast never requires a move, takes the bilateral gap from 375bp to 400bp and possibly 425bp without the franc leg contributing anything at all. Two scheduled decisions inside the horizon can prove it: the 5 November MPR, which carries a projection round and therefore moves the pair harder than a bare statement, and the 17 December MPC. The counterweight is dated and real. The 10 December SNB assessment is the only Swiss policy communication in the window and the market puts roughly even odds on a hike there; if the SNB validates the curve rather than its own forecast, the single largest input to this view inverts, the Swiss 2-year goes above 0.50% and the carry case contracts at the exact moment the sterling fiscal story is still unresolved. Our base case is a hold with no tightening signal, consistent with the Swiss Bankers Association survey in which 60% of respondents see no change through 2027, which would take 19bp of embedded hike pricing out of the Swiss front end and widen the measured differential further. Confidence is 68 rather than higher because the level of the carry is certain while its direction of travel depends on a coin-flip meeting the market has already half-priced.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is working on this specific pair and is not working on sterling generally. The regime is a benign-volatility, synchronised-tightening one in which the lowest-yielding G10 currency is borrowed and the fourth-highest-yielding one is held; VIX at 16.07, investment-grade spreads at 83bp and swap-line usage of USD 72mn describe exactly the conditions under which funding-currency shorts are paid. tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two economies sit at opposite corners of the inflation-growth grid and the corners cancel over four weeks. On inflation the gap is enormous and stable: UK headline 3.1% against Swiss 0.8%, UK core 2.6% against Swiss 0.4%, a 220bp core differential that is the widest in the G10 pair set. On growth the ranking inverts: Switzerland grew 1.885% quarter on quarter and 2.632% year on year in Q2 against the UK's 0.5% and 1.4%, the KOF barometer printed 109.1 in September against a 105.8 consensus and a five-year high, and the procure.ch PMI at 57.1 beat its forecast, while the UK's September flash composite fell to 51.7 from 52.5. So the base currency has the inflation that justifies the rate advantage and the quote currency has the growth. The pair-specific point is that the inflation differential is already being monetised through Factor 1 — it is the reason the differential is 375bp — so counting it again here would be double-counting; what Factor 2 proper contributes is the growth and relative-real-purchasing-power channel, and that channel favours the franc. A 230bp headline inflation differential erodes roughly 1.15% of sterling's relative purchasing power over six months against a nominal carry of 1.88%, so more than half the carry is given back in relative price terms. Both dossiers independently score their own tactical Factor 2 as Neutral, and asymmetric data sensitivity is modest: UK September CPI on 21 October is the one release in the window with the power to move the pair materially, and Swiss CPI is a low-amplitude event because core at 0.40% and wage growth at 0.40% leave the SNB's reaction function dormant whatever prints.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the growth and real-income channel turns against the pair while the inflation channel keeps paying through Factor 1, and on balance the former wins by a narrow margin. The mechanism is dated: Cornwall Insight forecasts the January 2027 Ofgem cap at GBP 1,999, a 16% and GBP 276 rise announced in late November, set against UK real regular pay growth of only +0.6% on a CPIH basis, which turns UK real household income growth negative in the first quarter of 2027. There is no Swiss counterpart to that shock — energy is roughly 3.5% of the Swiss basket against about 7% in the euro area, which is why an energy impulse that took US CPI to 3.4% and euro-area HICP to 3.2% lifted Swiss headline only to 0.8%. Meanwhile the UK labour market is loosening — payrolled employees down 101,000 year on year, vacancies 702,000, claimant count up 27,800 in August against 8,300 expected — while Swiss registered unemployment is stable at 3.1% and SECO has raised 2026 growth to 1.7%. The honest qualifications are two. SECO itself attributes roughly half of Q2 Swiss growth to the volatile chemical-pharmaceutical sector and expects second-half moderation, and the ZEW expectations index collapsed from 12.1 to 2.6 on 30 September, so the Swiss growth lead is less secure than the level suggests. And a UK slowdown that is driven by an energy cost shock is precisely the configuration that forces the BoE higher, which supports the pair through the carry leg. Confidence is 52 because those two offsets are genuine, not rhetorical.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically and Bearish strategically because the offsetting forces run on different clocks. Over four weeks the Swiss growth lead is loud and the UK inflation overshoot is loud, and they cancel inside one 21 October print. Over one to six months the UK real-income shock becomes a dated, quantified event through the late-November Ofgem announcement while the Swiss growth lead merely moderates, so the balance tips against the pair. The inflection is the Ofgem announcement, which converts a forecast into an arithmetic certainty.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: GBP/CHF is a moderate-beta risk pair with a pure haven on the quote side and a mildly risk-positive, domestically fragile currency on the base side — the framework's own classification places EUR/CHF in the moderate band and GBP/CHF belongs beside it, a reading corroborated by a retail aggregator that names global risk sentiment as the pair's dominant driver. The current cross-asset tape denies the franc the only mechanism that overrides a 375bp carry: VIX closed at 16.07 on 28 September, in the lower third of its distribution and up only 1.64 points on the month; the S&P 500 is up roughly 14% year to date and within 2% of its record; US investment-grade spreads are 83bp. Gold corroborates from the other direction, down 6.00% on the month, and since the franc's commodity link runs through shared safe-haven demand rather than trade, a falling gold price is a falling franc premium measured twice. Two counterweights are live and both sit on the quote side's ledger. US high-yield spreads widened 42bp on the month to 302bp, which is credit beginning to price the rate shock, and the OAT-Bund spread at 111.2bp is at the very top of its one-year range against a 74.2bp average with a EUR 54bn French budget vote pending — and the franc, not the euro, is the regional refuge from that. The pair-specific asymmetry worth stating plainly is that the base currency's own crisis correlation compounds rather than offsets: in a gilt sell-off sterling falls with yields rather than being supported by them, and the same event bids the franc, so GBP/CHF has a fatter left tail than a simple risk beta implies.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk channel is genuinely two-sided for this pair and the honest answer is no directional content. The constructive case is that the modal path is a continuation of the current expansion — tight credit, equities near highs, central banks tightening into full employment rather than easing into recession — and in that world the franc stays unbid while sterling collects its carry. The destructive case is that the base rate of a volatility event inside six months is materially above zero and that this specific pair pays for one twice: the franc's convexity is documented and extreme, with the January 2015 floor removal moving EUR/CHF roughly 30% intraday as the reference case, while sterling is the most duration-exposed G10 currency with roughly a quarter to 30% of gilts held abroad and the largest term premium in the block. A single risk shock therefore hits both legs in the same direction. Two identifiable triggers sit in the window: the French budget and a possible French government collapse, where the franc is the regional refuge, and the Iran negotiation, which is genuinely symmetric for this pair because escalation bids the franc while raising UK gas costs, and settlement removes the franc's haven bid while cutting the UK's January cap forecast. Expectation-weighted, the modal path is pair-positive and the tail is sharply pair-negative, which is the definition of a Neutral stance with real content rather than an absence of one. The weight falls to 0.05 strategically, so this is a small line either way.

tactical.unwind_trigger: Two triggers, pulling opposite ways. Either reporter gives the same sign: the UK is the deficit partner bilaterally as well as globally.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is the largest single argument against the pair and it is the cleanest contrast available in G10 outside Norway. Switzerland's 9.198%-of-GDP surplus is structurally composed — a goods surplus from pharmaceuticals and precision manufacturing, a services surplus from financial services and commodity trading, and a primary income surplus on CHF 5,564bn of foreign assets — and it is the mechanism behind the franc's multi-decade real appreciation. The UK's deficit is the mirror image and is deteriorating in its most dangerous component: primary income swung to a GBP 3.8bn quarterly deficit because a 93.8%-of-GDP debt stock funded at a 5.42% 10-year with roughly a quarter of gilts held abroad pays an ever-larger investment income bill overseas, which is a self-reinforcing external drag for as long as yields stay at 1999 auction highs. The terms-of-trade leg points the same way and is dated. UK NBP gas at 182.89p a therm is up 128.58% year on year and feeds the January Ofgem cap mechanically; Switzerland imports energy too but at roughly 3.5% of its basket, with producer and import prices running at -0.70% year on year. Valuation does not rescue the base currency either: sterling's BIS real effective rate of 112.33 is the third richest of eleven while the franc's 99.87 is seventh and 2.83% lower year on year, so on relative real terms the cross is carrying an expensive deficit currency against a cheapening surplus one. Confidence is 68 because the surplus and the deficit are measured rather than forecast; it is held below 70 because an Iran settlement would cut the gas term sharply and because structural flows cap rather than reverse a 441bp carry.

net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework's direction rules leg by leg. Oil up: moderately negative for GBP as an importer, mildly negative for CHF as a much less energy-intensive importer, and positive for CHF via the haven channel if the move is conflict-driven — net bearish GBP/CHF. Natural gas up: strongly negative for GBP through the Ofgem cap and the import bill, close to neutral for CHF — clearly bearish GBP/CHF, and this is the dominant term given the 128.58% annual rise. Gold up: positive for CHF through safe-haven correlation, neutral for GBP — bearish GBP/CHF; gold being down 6.00% on the month is therefore the one commodity currently helping the pair. Netting the three with gas dominant, the commodity complex is net bearish GBP/CHF, and the netting is unusually clean because the quote currency has no export commodity to offset the base currency's import exposure.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance divergence is as wide as the rate differential and points the same way. The MPC has achieved the hardest thing in central bank communication — moving market pricing from effectively no hike by December to close to 80% for 5 November without raising rates — using a 6-3 vote with three members backing 4.00%, a projection of CPI slightly over 4% in early 2027, an explicit judgement that inflation risks are tilted to the upside, and a Deputy Governor who voted to hold then said policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist. The SNB by design says almost nothing: four assessments a year, a three-member Governing Board, no dots, no rate path, and a conditional forecast whose entire message is that nothing needs to be done. The single most important communication change of the period was on the quote side and it is pair-positive — in June the SNB said its willingness to intervene should remain increased, and in September it reverted to the standard formulation of being willing to be active as necessary, dropping the qualifier while the franc depreciated roughly 3% trade-weighted. A central bank removing an elevated-intervention flag into a weakening currency is signalling comfort with that weakness, which is the clearest guidance asymmetry available between these two legs. Sequencing reinforces it: the base leg's event comes first and is the bigger one, with the 5 November MPR carrying a projection round, while the quote leg has no scheduled communication for seventy days. The offsets are the BoE's two-voice committee, with Taylor publicly downplaying the hiking case in the same week Lombardelli talked it up, and a 30bp miss on its own August CPI forecast.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the weight nearly doubles to 0.12 and the divergence persists, but both legs acquire a dated way of being wrong, which is why confidence falls three points rather than rising. On the base side the BoE's institutional architecture is strong — published individual votes, two Monetary Policy Reports with fan charts inside the window, and a unanimous decision to run gilt holdings to zero on a published schedule to 2034 that removed an annually contested vote from the gilt calendar. The specific strategic risk is the MPR convention itself: because the Report conditions its projections on market-implied rates, a November or February fan chart showing inflation at or below target on a 39bp-hike curve is the Bank telling the market its pricing is too hawkish, which would be a dovish shock to the base leg from the Bank's own publication. On the quote side the SNB's credibility is the best inflation record in the developed world and its forecast extends to 0.8% in 2028 on an unchanged rate, so the strategic question is simply whether the market or the central bank is right about 10 December. We side with the SNB and with the 60% of Swiss Bankers Association respondents who see no change through 2027, which would take roughly 19bp out of the Swiss front end and support the pair. Note too that at 0.00% the SNB has no conventional easing room, so a strengthening franc would be met with intervention rather than cuts — a weaker deterrent, which is part of why the curve retains hike optionality. Net: guidance divergence remains pair-positive, with one identifiable dovish risk on each leg.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the factor where the pair is most asymmetric, and the asymmetry is against it. The 28 October Autumn Budget and OBR Economic and Fiscal Outlook is the largest dated binary in G10 FX this month and it sits entirely on the base leg: the OBR's March headroom of GBP 23.6bn has been eroded by roughly GBP 24bn of rate, inflation, migration and unfunded-policy adjustments, it is the first Budget of an administration whose Prime Minister moved the 30-year gilt 9bp with the single word flexibility, and it lands into a market where the 30-year is 5.96% and the 29 September 10-year auction cleared at the highest borrowing cost since 1999. Switzerland contributes nothing on the other side — no federal election inside the horizon, a stable government, and the EU Bilaterals III package not expected to enter force until end-2028. The pair-specific point is that the two legs do not merely fail to offset, they compound: the quote currency is what capital buys when European risk spikes, so a disorderly Budget hits sterling directly and bids the franc at the same time. The French binary works the same way in the same window — OAT-Bund at 111.2bp is at a one-year high with a EUR 54bn budget vote pending, and the franc rather than the euro is the regional refuge. Options corroborate on the base leg, with 67% of Budget-week GBP/USD expiries bearish on sterling against a 55% baseline and roughly three-quarters of a heavier EUR/GBP concentration bearish. The one genuinely two-sided item is Iran, which is amplified rather than asymmetric: escalation hits the base through gas and bids the quote through haven demand, settlement helps the base through gas and hurts the quote twice over.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the widest sovereign quality differential available anywhere in G10 and it is entirely against the base currency. The UK carries public sector net debt of GBP 2,985.5bn, 93.8% of GDP, with August borrowing GBP 3.5bn above the OBR profile and the financial year to date GBP 8.1bn above it; central government debt interest of GBP 8.8bn in August was the highest August on record since 1997, including GBP 2.1bn of RPI-driven uplift on index-linked gilts, which is the mechanism that converts a UK inflation overshoot into immediate deficit. Ratings are AA from S&P, Aa3 from Moody's and AA from DBRS. Switzerland is AAA or Aaa from all five agencies with stable outlooks, general government gross debt of 38.5% of GDP falling toward 33.5% by 2031, a zero federal budget balance and a constitutional debt brake that makes the path a rule rather than a forecast. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar conditions reach this cross through the role each currency plays in the global funding chain rather than through a direct leg, and the two roles are opposite. The franc is the G10's funding currency — the lowest policy rate in the block by 125bp — so it is borrowed and converted whenever dollars are expensive but available. Sterling, at the fourth-highest policy rate in the block, is a carry destination rather than a funding currency, which the sterling brief states explicitly. Current conditions are the textbook configuration for that asymmetry: the Fed raised to 3.75-4.00% on 16 September, the broad dollar index stands at 120.33 and rose 1.88 points on the month, the US 10-year rose 51bp to 5.24% — dollars are expensive. But they are not scarce: SOFR printed 3.90%, exactly at interest on reserve balances, central bank liquidity swaps outstanding are USD 72mn, which is effectively nil, and no official counterparty anywhere is paying up for dollars. Expensive-but-abundant dollars is precisely the regime in which funding-currency shorts are paid and carry destinations are held, which is mildly pair-positive. The cross-currency basis is a documented gap on both legs — no free quoted series resolved for GBP/USD or CHF/USD — and the nearest proxy is the pair's own futures roll of 441.4bp against a 375bp policy differential, leaving roughly 66bp of combined basis-and-term residual that cannot be decomposed without an OIS curve. The single reserve-tightening signal is real and worth monitoring: reserve balances fell USD 83.6bn in the week to 23 September and USD 72.0bn year on year, with SOFR at rather than below interest on reserve balances.

That switches off the reserve drain and removes the single most powerful mechanism by which a funding currency — the franc — appreciates, while also removing the stress channel through which UK banks' large structural dollar funding needs would transmit to sterling. Set against that, reserve balances have still fallen USD 72.0bn over the year with SOFR printing at rather than below interest on reserve balances, and year-end balance-sheet constraints fall squarely inside the horizon. Turn-of-year funding pressure historically widens cross-currency basis and squeezes low-yielding funding currencies higher, and it would land within days of the 10 December SNB assessment, so the two quote-leg upside risks are correlated in timing. Both source dossiers independently go Neutral or near-neutral on this factor strategically, and the net pair effect of a dollar that has stopped tightening its balance sheet while year-end approaches is a genuine standoff rather than a weak lean. tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights the book is dominated by Policy and Rates at 0.27, Inflation and Growth at 0.18, Risk Appetite at 0.10 and Flows at 0.10, and the first of those decides the call. The bilateral policy differential is 375bp, the widest positive carry sterling earns anywhere and the third widest the franc pays, and the executable futures roll of 441.4bp means a rolled long is paid roughly 0.37% a month to wait, which is a cushion few G10 crosses offer. Neither central bank meets inside the four-week window — the gated file puts the BoE at 5 November and the SNB at 10 December — so the differential can only be repriced by data, and the two front ends carry asymmetric decay risk: the Swiss 2-year has added 19bp of hike pricing that the SNB's own conditional forecast of 0.7, 0.8 and 0.8 per cent on an unchanged rate says is unnecessary, while the UK front end is merely over-hawkish about a hike the Committee has already signalled through a 6-3 vote and a Deputy Governor's conditional pre-announcement. The two standalone dossier views reinforce rather than conflict at this horizon: sterling is Bearish at -0.0583 and the franc is Bearish at -0.3002, so the cross inherits a positive differential of roughly 0.24, and our independent bilateral score of +0.2309 lands on the same number by a different route. Three bilateral factors modify the standalone views materially. Guidance divergence is wider than the rate gap, because the SNB dropped its increased-intervention qualifier in September while the franc was depreciating, which is a central bank signalling comfort with a weaker currency against a central bank actively talking its own market into a hike. The risk tape denies the franc the only mechanism that overrides a 375bp carry, with VIX at 16.07, investment-grade spreads at 83bp and gold down 6% on the month. And the funding regime — expensive but abundant dollars, SOFR exactly at interest on reserve balances, swap lines at USD 72mn — is the configuration that pays funding-currency shorts and rewards carry destinations, which is what these two currencies respectively are. What is priced against what we expect is the edge: forwards discount the pair 4.4% a year purely as the uncovered-interest-parity offset, realised spot has contradicted that convention repeatedly, and aggregated bank research has the pair materially lower by year-end, so the market is paid to be wrong in the same direction we are paid to be right. The path of least resistance is a carry grind rather than a trend, and it has a dated interruption: 28 October brings the Budget, the OBR forecast and the FOMC in one session, and because the quote currency is the thing capital buys when risk spikes, a disorderly Budget hits both legs the same way. Other dated catalysts are 21 October (UK September CPI, the last inflation print before the Budget and the MPC), the French budget vote in the second week of October, and 5 November (BoE MPC and Monetary Policy Report), which sits just beyond a four-week window — so a tactical position carries the Budget without being paid for the MPR. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the score is concentrated in one factor, because the pair is the most extended cross in the sterling complex at the 97th close percentile, and because the single largest tail — a UK fiscal accident — moves both legs against the position simultaneously. It is 3 rather than 2 because the carry is measured, the guidance divergence is documented in both central banks' own words, and no scheduled event inside the window can narrow the differential.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net of +0.0398 falls inside the -0.10 to +0.10 band, so the derived stance is Neutral and is applied mechanically. The number is not a weak signal, it is a near-perfect standoff: gross positive contributions of +0.2496 from Policy and Rates and Guidance against gross negatives of -0.2098 from External Balance, Inflation and Growth, and Fiscal Risk. Four factors score zero, including USD Liquidity at a 0.09 weight and Risk Appetite, Flows and Market Structure. The interpretation is specific and worth stating rather than softening: over one to six months the pair is paid 400bp a year to hold an expensive, deficit, fiscally stressed currency against a cheap, surplus, AAA one, and the arithmetic says those two things very nearly cancel. A Neutral built from large opposing forces is less stable than one built from genuine absence of signal, and it should be read as a view that will resolve decisively once the December cluster passes rather than as a forecast of a quiet market.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the book changes shape rather than direction. Policy and Rates holds 0.27 but External Balance rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and Guidance from 0.07 to 0.12, while Inflation and Growth falls to 0.10 and Flows to 0.06 — so structural factors displace data-flow factors, and the result is a collision between the two largest of them. The carry case strengthens: a Bank Rate of 4.00% delivered on 5 November against an SNB that its own three-year conditional forecast says need never move takes the differential to 400bp and possibly 425bp without the franc leg contributing anything, which is worth +0.1836, the largest single line in the table. The structural case against is almost exactly as large. Switzerland runs a current account surplus of 9.198% of GDP with a net international investment position of CHF 986bn and a Q2 surplus that widened CHF 13bn year on year; the UK runs a 2.5%-of-GDP deficit whose most dangerous component, primary income, has swung to a GBP 3.8bn quarterly deficit precisely because a 93.8%-of-GDP debt stock funded at a 5.42% 10-year with a quarter of gilts held abroad pays an ever-larger bill overseas. Add a terms-of-trade shock that acts on one leg only — UK NBP gas up 128.58% year on year, feeding a January cap 16% higher, against a Swiss energy weight of roughly 3.5% — and a two-to-three notch rating gap, and the external and fiscal factors together contribute -0.158. The two standalone dossiers converge at this horizon in a way they do not tactically: sterling is Bearish at -0.0915 and the franc at -0.2566, a differential of +0.165, but that naive differencing double-counts the external balance, which is a negative in the sterling dossier and a positive in the franc dossier and is therefore counted once here, at -0.1088. That single correction is most of the gap between +0.165 and +0.0398, and it is the right correction to make in a bilateral frame. What is priced against what we expect: the market prices roughly 75bp of SNB tightening that the SNB's own forecast and 60% of a Swiss Bankers Association survey both reject, which is the clearest unpriced positive; and it prices sterling with no fiscal risk premium against a 1998-high 30-year gilt, which is the clearest unpriced negative. Aggregated bank research has the pair around 2.9% lower by end-2026 and 4.1% lower by Q1 2027, so our Neutral is materially above consensus without being bullish. The path of least resistance is a carry-supported range rather than a trend, and the dated sequence that resolves it is 28 October (Budget, OBR and FOMC), 5 November (BoE MPC and Monetary Policy Report), late November (Ofgem's January cap announcement), 10 December (SNB assessment, the quote leg's only scheduled communication in the horizon) and 17 December (BoE MPC). Conviction is 2 because the Neutral is the residual of two forces each worth roughly a fifth of the scale, so being wrong means being wrong about which of two correct observations dominates — a slow and expensive way to be wrong. It is not 1 because the two forces are measured rather than forecast, and the dates on which they resolve are known.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically GBP/CHF loses its tactical distinction. The GBP dossier ranks sterling 8th of 11 and the CHF dossier ranks the franc 9th of 11 over one to six months, so the gap between the legs closes to almost nothing — which is precisely why the score is Neutral. As a sterling long it ranks behind GBP/CAD, where the Bank of Canada's core is at target and the entry is at the 74th range percentile rather than the 97th. As a franc short it ranks behind USD/CHF, which carries comparable carry without a dated fiscal binary on its base leg, and behind AUD/CHF at 460bp. Its one durable distinction is that it is the cleanest pure carry-versus-external-balance trade in G10: nowhere else does the widest sterling carry meet the second-largest current account surplus in the block.

strategic.path_expectation: Expect a range-bound path with three nodes, not a trend. The first is the tactical leg into November, likely toward 1.1000–1.1050 if the Budget disappoints without breaking. The second runs from late November to mid-December: the Ofgem cap announcement, the 9 December FOMC, the 10 December SNB and the 17 December MPC within four weeks of each other. This is where the Neutral resolves, and it coincides with year-end funding pressure that historically favours funding currencies, so a pullback into 1.0850–1.0900 (around the 100-day average, likely to have risen toward roughly 1.09 by then) is the most probable December shape. The third node, in the first quarter of 2027, is where the UK real-income shock becomes measurable and the external-balance factor takes over. The pair should drift lower toward 1.0950 unless the Iran settlement or Budget-credibility upside has fired by then. The 200-week average stays a ceiling throughout and only falls to about 1.0999 by end-March, so a sustained break above it requires one of the upside conditions, not just time. Over two to four weeks the 375bp policy differential and 441bp executable roll, a benign risk tape that denies the franc a haven bid, a guidance divergence in which the SNB has signalled comfort with depreciation while the BoE has talked its market into a hike, and a funding regime of expensive-but-abundant dollars together outweigh a one-sided fiscal binary on 28 October. Over one to six months a carry that widens to 400bp is almost exactly offset by an 11.7 percentage point current account differential, a two-to-three notch rating gap and a gas-driven terms-of-trade shock that acts on the base leg alone. consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Above consensus on both horizons. Consensus is outright bearish the pair; we are Bullish tactically and Neutral strategically, so the divergence is one full stance step tactically and one strategic.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Stated in stance and score terms: the aggregated bank consensus implies roughly 2.9% of pair downside by end-2026 and 4.1% by Q1 2027, against our Neutral strategic score of +0.0398 and a forward curve that itself discounts the pair 4.41% annualised. Our strategic Neutral is above both the consensus path and the forward path, while our tactical Bullish is above both by a wider margin. In levels (second pass): roughly 280 pips above consensus at end-2026 and about 420 pips above the Q1 2027 consensus of 1.0533.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three bilateral factors we weigh differently. First, consensus treats the SNB's no-change path as neutral for the franc when it is in fact the removal of a priced hike cycle: the Swiss 2-year has added 19bp on roughly 75bp of embedded 2027 tightening that the SNB's own conditional forecast, built explicitly on an unchanged 0% rate, says is unnecessary, and 60% of a Swiss Bankers Association survey agrees with the central bank rather than the curve. Second, consensus appears to price the pair off the forward curve, and the forward discount of 441bp is an uncovered-interest-parity convention, not a forecast — realised spot has contradicted it repeatedly, and treating it as an expectation is the single most common error in high-carry cross forecasting. Third, we weigh the guidance asymmetry more heavily than consensus does: the SNB dropping its increased-intervention qualifier in September while the franc depreciated roughly 3% trade-weighted is a central bank declaring comfort with a weaker currency, and it has no equivalent on the sterling side, where the Committee is actively steering pricing higher. Where we agree with consensus, and say so, is strategically: the external balance and fiscal differentials are real, large and ultimately binding, which is why our six-month score is Neutral rather than Bullish. Second-pass supplement: the consensus is less one-sided than the averages imply. Bank of America has argued the uptrend has further to run, partly based on the SNB's intervention stance restricting franc strength; since then the SNB has dropped the "increased" qualifier, which reinforces our Factor 6 reading. UBS frames the same risk from the franc's side. The bearish end of the range is MUFG's long-standing 1.02 sell target, dated April. The consensus average therefore mixes stale bearish targets with more recent carry-positive views, and the spot has outrun most of it. Two developments since the first pass are recorded without re-scoring: Swiss September CPI printed 1.0% headline and 0.5% core, in line with expectations, and excluding petroleum products inflation was unchanged at 0.3% YoY, which supports the view that the SNB will not validate the curve; and cooler US PCE data lowered the implied probability of an October Fed rate hike from nearly 51% to about 38%, which slightly weakens the expensive-dollar funding argument in Factor 10.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the tactical view is right the pair holds or rises through the 28 October and 5 November cluster while a rolled long additionally collects roughly 0.37% a month in carry, and the gap to a consensus looking for 2.9% of downside by year-end is the measure of the repricing available. The larger payoff is in the Swiss front end rather than the cross: a 10 December hold with no tightening signal would take the Swiss 2-year back toward 0.15% in a market that has been one-way for a month.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The loss is fast rather than slow and arrives through a single channel. A disorderly Budget on 28 October hits the base leg directly and bids the quote leg simultaneously, and because the pair sits at the 97th percentile of its one-year closing range (85th on the payload) with no listed option and no quoted hedge on the cross, the move would be a gap rather than a grind. The secondary risk is the 10 December SNB validating the curve, which would invert the largest single input to the strategic view at the exact moment year-end funding pressure independently squeezes funding currencies higher. Where this second pass disagrees with the settled verdict: the direction stands; the disagreement is about size and shape. The tactical Bullish score rests 76% on one factor, and once levels are mapped the base case pays a third of what the downside case costs before carry. The first pass also scored Factor 9 against a 97th closing percentile and 4.80% realised volatility, whereas the payload shows 85th and 5.38% and a fresh rejection at the ten-touch 1.10955–1.11969 band on the 52-week-high day, which makes the structural caution stronger, not weaker. Recommendation: implement the Bullish call at half the standard conviction-3 size, buying dips rather than chasing, and treat a daily close below 1.0849 as evidence that the pair-specific negatives (event, fiscal, structure) have outweighed the carry sooner than the score assumes.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because the two dominant forces operate on different clocks and the heavier one arrives later. Tactically the 375bp carry is collected in a tape that gives the franc no haven bid, no Swiss policy communication is scheduled for seventy days, and the external and fiscal differentials — which are the whole of the bearish case — carry only 0.10 of combined weight. Strategically External Balance alone rises from 0.06 to 0.16 and Fiscal Risk from 0.04 to 0.07, so the same unchanged facts about an 11.7 percentage point current account gap, a two-to-three notch rating gap and a gas shock that acts on one leg only acquire 0.23 of combined weight and very nearly cancel a carry that is itself widening. Three factors change stance across the horizons and in each case the change is against the pair: Inflation and Growth from Neutral to Bearish as the January real-income shock becomes dated, External Balance from Neutral to Bearish as cumulative flows start to matter, and Event Risk from Bearish to Neutral — the one change in the pair's favour, and only because the Budget discharges inside the tactical window.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The sequence 28 October to 10 December, with the 5 November Bank of England MPC and Monetary Policy Report as the pivot. Before it the pair is a carry trade with a dated fiscal interruption; after it Bank Rate is probably 4.00% and the differential is realised rather than expected, at which point the binding question becomes whether an 11.7 percentage point external differential and a 93.8%-of-GDP debt stock can be out-earned at 400bp a year. The late-November Ofgem announcement converts the UK real-income shock from forecast to arithmetic, and the 10 December SNB assessment — the quote leg's only scheduled communication in either horizon — resolves roughly 75bp of embedded Swiss hike pricing in one direction or the other.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical Bullish and the strategic Neutral as one position with a defined life rather than as two conflicting views. The carry is worth owning into and through the November decision because no scheduled event can narrow the differential before then and the roll pays about 0.37% a month to wait. It is not worth owning blind through the December cluster, where two independent quote-leg positives — a possible SNB validation of the curve and year-end funding pressure that squeezes funding currencies — land within days of each other and coincide with the UK energy cap announcement. Express the tactical leg in spot, where the carry is collected and the estimated option surface is too uncertain to pay for; express any strategic exposure with optionality assembled from the dollar legs, accepting the basis risk, because the cross itself has no listed option and the franc's convexity means a naked spot long is implicitly short a cheap one. Second-pass level mapping: the tactical position runs from the 1.0930–1.0975 entry zone to 1.1050–1.1150; if 1.1050 or above is reached before 5 November, take half off before the MPR; from late November, scale back to the strategic carry-hold size, reduce into the ten-touch band rather than adding, and do not hold the full tactical size into 10 December; if the pair is below 1.0849 on any daily close before then, the tactical leg is closed and the strategic carry hold resizes against the 1.0700 weekly stop.

assumptions: Price series as delivered. The payload reports dataPoints 130, dateRange "2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02", spot 1.09734 and spotDate "2026-10-02". The dataQuality line is reproduced verbatim: "GBP/CHF: 4901 weekday bars in the store (2007-12-21 to 2026-10-02); 1007 weekly, 500 monthly; 130 daily bars passed downstream (2026-04-06 to 2026-10-02), which is the 1-6 month strategic horizon". The computationRange for averages and zones is 2007-12-21 to 2026-10-02 (4,901 weekday bars), with zero weekend bars dropped.

Spot date gap. The spotDate of 2026-10-02 is one trading session AFTER the 2026-10-01 valuation date. Every level, pip distance, percentage and forward in this report is anchored to 1.09734. The base dossier's GBP/CHF figure of 1.10319 (2026-09-29 close) is superseded. No web-quoted spot was used.

Moving averages. All are simple averages of trading-day closes (weekday bars only). The 200-week average is 1.10362, sloping −0.000143 a week, with the last weekly close above it three weeks ago. Its value after 26 weeks (about 1.0999) is a linear extrapolation of the stated slope.
Zone distances. Zone distances are the payload's own figures, measured from spot to each zone's midpoint. Zones are ranked by touch count, not by distance.

Realised and implied volatility. Realised volatility is the payload's 20-day 5.65% and 60-day 5.38%, annualised on 252 days. Implied volatility is the store's triangle estimate (5.095%, 4.969% and 5.198% at 36.7, 99.7 and 190.6 days, observed 2026-09-30). It is an ESTIMATE that runs low. The bias-adjusted figures (about 5.7–5.9%) apply the store's 14.4% median shortfall and are illustrative only. No IV percentile or risk reversal exists for the cross.

Forward outrights. Forwards are derived from the −441.4bp futures roll using a linear convention (spot × (1 − 0.04414 × t)), not quoted. The roll embeds cross-currency basis and is not a policy differential.

Rate block. The policy differential of 3.75 is as of 2026-09-28 for GBP and 2026-09-29 for CHF. The payload's 10-year yields (GBP 4.9886%, CHF 0.47%) are MONTHLY series as of 2026-08-01 and are not quoted as live levels. Live prints from the dossiers (gilt 5.42%, Confederation 0.58%) are named as such where used.

Verdict carried, not re-derived. The factors, stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, weighted contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, G10 rankings, consensus divergence and cross-horizon consistency are carried verbatim from the pass-1 Direction Verdict and were not re-scored. Where the price payload contradicts an input pass 1 used (Factor 9's 97th percentile and 4.80% realised volatility), the contradiction is recorded in clearly marked second-pass notes, and the scored record is left unchanged.

What this pass sets. Scenario probabilities follow the framework's 50/25/25 convention and are subjective. Scenario targets are anchored to the payload's computed zones and moving averages. Entries, stops and sizing are this pass's own and use ATR(14) of 66 pips as the unit.

Carry in risk/reward. Roll accruals of about 37 pips over four weeks and 242 pips over six months assume the −441.4bp roll is constant. They are reported separately from spot payoffs so that the spot view and the carry view are never confused.

Bilateral trade. IMF DOTS 2024 figures come from the supplied block and were not re-estimated. The mirror asymmetry (Swiss-reported exports to the UK of USD 22.6bn against UK-reported imports from Switzerland of USD 12.8bn) is read as non-monetary gold routed through London.

Citation numbering. Citations 1–38 are the pass-1 verdict's sources, kept with their original numbering so the factor citation arrays remain valid. Citations 39–50 are new sources accessed in this pass. Extrapolation-model forecast sites that appeared in search results were excluded as forecasts, consistent with pass 1. One community chart idea and one retail technical commentary are cited only for pattern and round-number context and are labelled as such.

Second-pass facts not in the scored record. Swiss September CPI (1.0% headline, 0.5% core) and the reduction in October Fed hike odds to about 38% were published around the valuation date. They are recorded as context and in catalysts only.

Data limitations in extraction: no CFTC percentile series or implied-volatility history exists for this cross, so positioning percentiles and the IV percentile are not available; the dossier dates are taken as the valuation date.
